new_statements.quote: Hadoti also displays three-way distinction in syllable weight with monomoraic light syllables, bimoraic heavy syllables, and trimoraic superheavy syllables. In Hadoti monosyllabic word has prominence while disyllabic word second syllable has prominence. It is because of the heaviness of the syllable weight, lengthening, and duration of the particular syllable. [...] In a disyllabic word, the heavy syllable gets prominence based on vowel or mora. [p. 125] ... In Hadoti stress marking is based on the syllable weight. In a disyllabic word, the send [sic] syllable has the syllable weight that is why it becomes the stressed syllable. [p. 136]

It is because of the heaviness of the syllable weight, lengthening, and duration of the particular syllable.' and (two sentences later) 'In a disyllabic word, the heavy syllable gets prominence based on vowel or mora.' new_statements.rule_in_words: One stress per word; the heavy syllable (by mora count: light V, heavy VV/VC, superheavy VVC/VCC) is stressed, following the Hindi-Urdu pattern (last heavy syllable, penult if all light); in the authors' disyllabic verb data this puts prominence on the heavier (second) syllable, and in reduplications with /rə/ on the reduplicant.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not described; the analysis assumes a One-Stress constraint ('only one stress at the word level'; two stressed syllables 'is not the feature of Hadoti language', p. 133).
new_statements.exceptions: In verbal reduplication the stressed syllable is on the base when no particle intervenes, but shifts to the reduplicant (rightmost) when the discourse marker /rə/ is inserted (pp. 126, 136-137); 'Sometimes it may vary according to syllable weight' (p. 126). Suffixation does not alter stress placement (p. 121).
new_statements.domain_note: Word level, but the evidence base is verbal reduplication forms (/kʰa rə kʰa/, /kʰato kʰato/) elicited in Kota (Nov-Dec 2015) and inspected with Praat pitch tracks; the general lexicon is not surveyed and the weight rule is adopted from Hussain (1997) for Hindi-Urdu (last heavy syllable stressed, else penult). Internally inconsistent: p. 121 says in disyllabic /kʰa.to/ the root /kʰa/ is prominent and the suffix /to/ is not, while p. 125 says the second syllable of a disyllable has prominence. p. 118: 'Stress is not prominent in Hadoti (like Hindi) as compared to the English language.'
new_statements.identity_note: Chand & Kar's 'Hadoti' is the Kota-region variety (fieldwork in Kota, Rajasthan, Nov-Dec 2015), which they call 'a regional variety of Hindi (Rajasthani)'; this is Harauti/Hadoti = hado1235 (Grierson's Harauti of Bundi, Kota, Jhalawar). Sharma 1954 separates Sipari from Hadoti proper.

sources.citation: Chand, Gulab & Somdev Kar (2017). Sonority and reduplication in Hadoti. Journal of Universal Language 18(2): 1-37. DOI 10.22425/jul.2017.18.2.1
sources.note: Syllable structure and sonority only (CV/CVC preferred; up to quadrisyllabic reduplications); no mention of stress, accent or prominence anywhere in the text.

sources.citation: Parihar, Ravi (2017). Review of Dwivedi, Amitabh Vikram (2012) A Grammar of Hadoti, Munich: Lincom Europa, 127 pp. Dialectologia 18: 189-203. DOI 10.1344/dialectologia2016.18.10
sources.note: Summarises the grammar's Chapter 2 'Phonology' (pp. 6-23): 36 consonants, 10 vowels, distribution, consonant clusters, phonemic contrasts, oral/nasal vowels, vowel clusters, syllable structure (CCCVCCC), syllable division. No mention of stress or accent in the summary of the chapter.

sources.citation: Dwivedi, Amitabh Vikram (2014). The status of Haroti: an enquiry into Rajastani language. Dialectologia 12: 53-65.
sources.note: Sociolinguistic/status paper; 'accent' used only in the lay sense of regional accent. Nothing on word stress.

sources.citation: Allen, W. S. (1957). Some phonological characteristics of Rajasthani. Bulletin of SOAS 20: 5-11 (sections 5-6 on the Harauti vowel system and vowel (dis)harmony).
sources.note: Harauti vowel inventory, tense/lax asymmetry, anaptyctic vowel, vowel-quality conditioning in disyllables. No statement about stress or prominence.

sources.citation: Sharma, Kanhaiyalal (1954). Hadoti boli aur sahitya [Hindi]. Udaipur: Rajasthan Sahitya Academy, 450 pp. Digital Library of India item 2015.308084.
sources.note: Chapter 'Hadoti dhvaniyan' (pp. 13-33) covers vowels (with a footnote citing W. S. Allen's lax/tense split), nasal vowels, vowel sequences, consonants by manner, consonant clusters. No balaghat/svaraghat (stress) heading in the table of contents and no stress statement found in the (noisy) scanned of the chapter.

sources.citation: Grierson, George A. (1908). Linguistic Survey of India, vol. IX pt. 2: Rajasthani and Gujarati. Harauti section, pp. 293ff.
sources.note: Harauti sketch: e for ai, readers postposition ne, pronouns; 'Saving for a few words peculiar to its vocabulary, Harauti does not otherwise differ... from Standard Jaipuri'. No stress statement (the volume's introductory note only explains the acute-accent convention in general).
